Rust on microcontrollers: no OS, no allocator required, and the same ownership rules that make systems code safe make firmware safe. Memory errors in firmware are bricked devices, so this is where Rust's guarantees pay off most.

The stack

Layer Crate Role
Language #![no_std] no standard library
HAL traits embedded-hal standard interfaces (GPIO, SPI, I2C)
Async HAL embedded-hal-async async versions
Chip support cortex-m, cortex-m-rt ARM Cortex-M runtime
PAC stm32f4xx-hal etc. register-level access
HAL embassy-stm32, rp2040-hal ergonomic per-chip drivers
Async runtime embassy-executor no-alloc async executor
Logging defmt deferred formatting, tiny binary size
Flashing probe-rs debug probe flashing + RTT logging
RTOS-ish rtic real-time scheduling with priorities

no_std vs std

You lose std's String, Vec (unless you add alloc with a heap), threads, files and networking. You gain a binary that fits in 16 KB and boots in microseconds.

panic_halt on panic: an infinite loop. Alternatives: panic_abort, panic_probe (prints over RTT then halts — the useful one while developing).

Blinky: the "hello world"

Gotcha: async on a microcontroller is not an OS. Timer::after(...).await suspends the task and the executor runs something else; there is no thread and no stack switch. Stack usage per task is fixed at compile time and a deep call chain in one task can still overflow the 2–8 KB you gave it.

embedded-hal: driver code that works everywhere

The reason the ecosystem is healthy: a driver written against embedded-hal traits works on every chip.

That function compiles for an STM32, an nRF52, an ESP32 and an RP2040 without change. This is what "traits instead of inheritance" buys you.

Reading a sensor over I2C

No allocation, no dynamic dispatch, fixed-size buffers on the stack. Everything is proven at compile time.

RTIC: real-time scheduling

RTIC gives you compile-time-verified interrupt priorities with no data races: the borrow checker enforces that two tasks cannot access a shared resource at conflicting priorities.

Firmware update (OTA) considerations

The parts people get wrong:

  1. A/B partitions. Flash two slots; write the new image to the inactive one, verify a checksum, flip a boot flag. Never overwrite the running image.
  2. Power loss mid-write must leave a bootable device. Write-then-verify-then- flip-flag is the only safe order.
  3. Signature verification before boot. An unsigned OTA endpoint is remote code execution for anyone who can reach the server.
  4. Rollback. Keep the previous image until the new one has run for N minutes.

Practical reality check

Concern Reality
Binary size Rust firmware is 5–20% larger than C, shrinking with opt-level="s" + LTO
Toolchain maturity excellent on Cortex-M and RISC-V; ESP32 and Xtensa also work
Debugging probe-rs + defmt is better than most C setups
Libraries fewer than C, but embedded-hal unifies what exists
Hiring fewer embedded Rust engineers, but they tend to be strong

Where Rust embedded is actually used

  • Espressif ships official Rust support for ESP32.
  • Microsoft Azure Sphere uses Rust for secure MCU apps.
  • Nordic supports Rust on nRF52/nRF53.
  • Automotive and industrial gateways: RTIC and embassy on Cortex-M.
  • Raspberry Pi Pico has first-class embassy-rp support.

Exercises

  1. Get blinky running on any dev board with probe-rs. If you have no hardware, run it under qemu-system-arm with the lm3s6965evb machine.
  2. Write a generic blink against embedded-hal traits and compile it for two different chips.
  3. Read a sensor's chip-id over I2C and print it with defmt::info!.
  4. Convert a polling loop into an embassy task with Timer::after.
  5. Explain why #![no_main] is required and what cortex_m_rt::entry provides.
  6. Design (on paper) an A/B OTA scheme with power-loss safety, and list the failure points.
